name: Refugee Status (Joint UNHCR / Ministry of Interior Registration)

requirements.blocker_text: Iraq has a domestic legal basis for political asylum -- the Political Refugee Act No. 51 of 1971 -- though its full operative text could not be independently confirmed in this build (the Refworld-hosted copy returned no machine-readable text). As of April 2026, registration has shifted from a UNHCR-only process to a JOINT process with the Ministry of Interior's Permanent Committee for Refugee Affairs (PC-MOI), led by Brigadier General Nadhim Abdullah Ahmed: applicants still book appointments through UNHCR's portal, but complete registration with Iraqi officials, who issue the identity card directly. Registration (around 15 minutes, with biometric data collection) confirms legal identity, reduces arrest/detention risk, and opens access to healthcare and education; mobile missions extend this beyond Baghdad. Without a valid UNHCR/PC-MOI certificate, a person is subject to ordinary Iraqi immigration law and risks deportation.
requirements.fix_path: Register with UNHCR's Iraq portal to book an appointment, then complete registration jointly with the Ministry of Interior's PC-MOI to receive the identity card.

outcome.duration_length: indefinite, tied to continued registration/protection needs

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Iraq). STATUS: DRAFT -- best sourcing reached tier 2 (UNHCR's own help portal); the Political Refugee Act's actual text (tier 2 on Refworld) could not be read (empty/non-machine-readable PDF), a genuine fetch limitation disclosed rather than papered over. GENUINE, VERY CURRENT STRUCTURAL FINDING: Iraq is in the middle of an ACTIVE, NAMED transition (started April 2026, five months before this build) from UNHCR-run registration to a joint UNHCR/Iraqi-government process under the Ministry of Interior's Permanent Committee for Refugee Affairs (PC-MOI) -- a genuinely more developed, actively-modernizing domestic structure than Algeria, Haiti, or Cuba (all built earlier in this dataset), each of which has NO domestic government body at all. This mirrors a stated global pattern (per the source) of countries like Ethiopia and Rwanda integrating refugee management into national identity systems. family_can_join set to false (schema requires a boolean here, not null) -- no derivative-family-registration mechanism was found in the sourcing, so false reflects no confirmed route rather than a confirmed denial. family_can_work left null: no rights information detailed enough to even guess conservatively -- a distinct, disclosed category of gap from files elsewhere in this dataset that DO confirm a restrictive default.
